Data mining techniques, particularly association rule mining, are extensively employed to extract patterns from data, such as market basket analysis. A key metric in this process is the confidence of an association rule, measured by the probability of its consequent given its antecedent. Researchers have long sought to identify a minimal set of high-confidence rules that can infer all other rules above a specified confidence threshold. This problem is complicated by the fact that, in infinite data domains, there can be an infinite number of high-confidence rules. To address this challenge, a new framework for reasoning with repetition and deduction has been developed, enabling more efficient and comprehensive association rule mining.

This study examines how mandating mental health treatment through court order impacts crime recidivism and the duration of incarceration. We focus on a policy implemented in a major US city that made mental health treatment compulsory for certain convicted individuals. We found that this policy led to significant improvements in the treatment of mental health issues and substance abuse, but also resulted in increased time spent in prison. Despite initial reductions in rearrests, these gains were eventually negated. We found that the policy had a greater positive effect on the recidivism rates of older and more educated individuals, as well as those with prior arrests, and that the improvements in non-violent rearrests were larger than those in violent rearrests. We found that the policy had no significant long-term impact on a person's earnings.

We introduce the Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials of a parametric type, along with its relevant properties, and then derive the Apostol-Bernoulli numbers of a parametric type as a special case. This is accomplished through the use of a complex number context and a new apostol-bernoulli expansion, which also enables us to establish various relationships, including a new identity, involving the apostol-bernoulli numbers and polynomials of a parametric type.

Radio maps are becoming an essential component in the design of wireless networks, providing a comprehensive overview of the available spectrum. However, gathering the necessary data for a radio map is a labor-intensive process that requires manual measurements, limiting its applicability to small areas. To address this challenge, a new approach combines drones with software-defined radios to map the spectrum more efficiently. By using an open-source framework, a collaborative system of drones and ground stations is coordinated to collect data, process it, and generate a radio map in near real-time. The proposed solution leverages the capabilities of software-defined radios to enable a scalable and cost-effective method for radio map acquisition.

To effectively identify unusual events in complex systems, we've developed a novel approach based on hidden Markov models for gauge pressure evaluations in technical setups. This method is capable of detecting anomalies in real-time, even in the presence of uncertain external influences. We've successfully applied and tested this model on a rotating equipment system, where it accurately pinpointed irregularities in real-time. Additionally, the system is currently being implemented in a wind turbine to identify gauge pressure irregularities and a fault in the rotor's revolution pattern.

This research explores the feasibility of using a combination of biometric features, including voice, face, and heat imaging, for individual verification. We conducted a comprehensive study, utilizing a database of 100 people, each providing a set of 10 audio-visual-thermal videos. Our investigation involved creating a multi-stage process for authentication, combining the analysis of voice, face, and heat imaging, and then validating the results using a heat-mapping technique. Our outcomes demonstrate that a combined approach yields the highest accuracy, with an error rate of 0.8%, and reveal that voice-based recognition offers the most precise results, with an error rate of 0.008%.

In the realm of automatic speech recognition, a common strategy for dealing with limited training data is to artificially expand it. This technique, known as data augmentation, has been successfully applied to image classification but has seen limited use in speech processing. Building on past efforts, our research presents a novel and simple method for increasing speech training data that surpasses existing techniques. This approach is particularly effective when paired with a neural network-based speech synthesizer, enabling it to produce a wide range of speech variations. We demonstrate that this method is versatile and can be used with various speech processing models, yielding more robust ASR models. In addition, we find that it also improves the performance of neural machine translation models trained with speech-text pairs.

When evaluating a combination of distributions, researchers often lack access to complete data and instead have limited samples drawn from each component. A statistical approach, known as a maximum likelihood estimator, has been developed to identify optimal mixing proportions, weights for the average of parameters, and the parameters of the individual components, based on the available sampled information. The validity of this estimator is supported by the convergence in probability of its components to their true values as the sample size increases, as well as the convergence in law of a specific transformation of its components. The asymptotic properties of 100% confidence intervals for the confidence levels have also been investigated. The usefulness of this estimator is demonstrated through numerical simulations and real-world data analysis.

In the pursuit of protecting sensitive information, researchers have turned to a principle known as differential privacy. Building on this foundation, a new concept called one-sided differential privacy has been developed, which offers robust confidentiality for independent data points. However, when these data points have underlying relationships, there is a potential risk of exposing individual information. Our research investigates this potential risk, which arises from the interdependence of data points, and provides a framework for quantifying the loss of confidentiality in such scenarios. Our findings reveal that one-sided differential privacy can be compromised when inferring a single data point from a single sample, even when multiple samples are provided. This theoretical limitation is further constrained by underlying characteristics, which can be quantified using a measure of robustness called one-sided differential robustness.

Our research focuses on the AS 209 protoplanetary disk, a system that exhibits multiple distinct ring and gap structures. We analyzed 12CO and 13CO emission lines at a resolution of approximately 20 astronomical units, revealing a significant reduction in gas content within an inner ring region. Our findings indicate that the gas-to-dust ratio in this region is 10 to 20 times lower than in other parts of the disk, suggesting either substantial gas loss or chemical alteration. Our analysis suggests that gas loss is the most likely explanation, given the lack of significant ionization and destruction of carbon monoxide. Our results imply that the ring and gap structures in AS 209 are formed by planet formation processes, and that the inner ring may be influenced by a planet with a mass of at least 0.15 times the mass of Jupiter. Our findings also suggest that the ring and gap structures in AS 209 are consistent with predictions from hydrodynamic simulations of planet-disk interactions.

We have developed an examination toolkit specifically designed for time-sequence tagged data, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of time-dependent measurements. This toolkit is versatile and can be applied to various fields such as chemistry, focusing on the dynamic behavior of molecules over time. It is implemented in Python and made freely available on the GitHub platform under the license of choice.

In this paper, we investigate a mean field game scenario with constraints on the state in a finite horizon setting, where the horizon is a fixed time period. The constraints are defined within a given compact set, and we assume that this set has a certain smooth boundary. Our analysis takes place in a setting with a fixed, finite time horizon.

Recent high-resolution data from the Gaia mission has enabled a thorough examination of the Galaxy's disk structure by analyzing its radial density variations. A key feature identified in previous studies is the presence of "stellar threads" - patterns that appear to extend across the disk. However, upon further analysis, many of these "threads" are found to be statistical artifacts resulting from specific data selection methods and not genuine structures. Although some "threads" may persist after accounting for these effects, their persistence does not necessarily imply a genuine underlying structure. Instead, many of these "threads" can be attributed to fluctuations inherent in random point patterns, such as those produced by Poisson processes. As such, further research is required to definitively establish the authenticity of these "stellar threads" and their potential significance in understanding the Galaxy's disk structure.

Current visual analysis techniques are primarily designed for detecting object-level differences, but they are not well-suited for visual discrepancy detection (VDD), which involves identifying subtle variations in visual styles. To address this challenge, we introduce a new task called Visual Discrepancy Detection (VDD), which focuses on identifying and categorizing minor visual differences within an image. To tackle this complex task, we develop a multi-stage approach that begins with pre-training on a large dataset of fashion images to capture fine-grained visual details, followed by fine-tuning with task-specific objectives. Our proposed method, named VICTOR, outperforms existing approaches by a significant margin on the FashionMNIST dataset and achieves promising results on the FGDNIST dataset, which was created specifically for the VDD task.

The concept of resource theories has significantly influenced the study of quantum technologies, offering a systematic method to analyze specific quantum states or operations that deviate from a set of freely accessible "free states" or "free operations." Research in resource theories has achieved notable successes in the areas of coherence, asymmetry, entanglement, and qubit nonclassicality. This article provides a comprehensive introduction to resource theories of light, focusing on multi-mode systems and exploring the foundational principles of resource theory construction. It also examines key examples, such as photon number statistics, cluster states, entanglement, nonlocality, and nonclassicality in multi-photon systems.

In federated learning, asynchronous gradient accumulation is a common technique used to accelerate model training. This method allows clients with different computation speeds to contribute without holding up faster ones. However, in the case of buffered accumulation, previous studies have not fully explored its behavior. This paper addresses a significant research gap by analyzing buffered accumulation in a non-iid setting, where clients' data is not uniformly distributed. By developing an asynchronous stochastic gradient descent algorithm and establishing its convergence rate, we provide theoretical guarantees. Our results show that buffered accumulation can introduce bias and noise, which in turn affects the convergence rate. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bias can be mitigated by adjusting the algorithm's parameters, and that the convergence rate can be comparable to that of immediate accumulation under certain conditions. Our findings are validated through experiments, which show that buffered accumulation can reduce communication costs and improve convergence in some scenarios.

This research paper builds upon operational calculus by creating a parallel calculus within the space of polynomial tempered distributions, represented as finite sequences of coefficients, where each corresponds to a specific derivative evaluation at the point 0. By reinterpreting key concepts such as distribution derivatives, smooth test function values, and convolution operations in terms of coefficient sequences, this study enables the derivation of operational formulas involving integrals and Laplace transforms.

A new constraint on the fraction of dark matter made up of primordial black holes is derived, which limits this fraction to less than 0.014 for PBHs with a mass of $10^{22}$ grams. This new bound results from applying the Swampland Distance Conjecture to the evolution of the scalar field that controls the fraction of dark matter constituted by PBHs.

Self-sustaining, thin, flexible structures called biological and synthetic vesicles, or membranes, typically form smooth, continuous surfaces. However, under certain conditions, these membranes can develop cracks, or fractures, which spread across their surfaces. The formation of fractures in these membranes is primarily driven by mechanical stress, but understanding the molecular processes that lead to fracture initiation and propagation is crucial. This knowledge has significant implications for interpreting membrane-related phenomena in biology and material science. This review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of membrane fracture mechanics, incorporating recent research findings, to facilitate further exploration of the topic.

Recent advancements in the synthesis of wurtzite-phase binary and ternary nitrides have led to the creation of new materials with unique properties. The development of ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ has enabled researchers to explore their potential in lattice-matching with GaN, which could lead to the growth of high-quality nitride heterostructures. Theoretical calculations have shown that aligning GaN with these two materials in an anisotropic strain results in significant increases in the hole effective mass and spin-orbit splitting energy. The spin-orbit splitting energy can be increased by up to 100% and 250% when GaN is strained with ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$, respectively. The increased hole mobility and spin-orbit interaction could lead to the development of new nitride material systems with enhanced performance for optoelectronic and spintronic applications.

Achieving effective navigation in the complex and dynamic environment of the sea poses a significant challenge for marine robots. To overcome this, a novel approach is proposed that utilizes a sparse Gaussian process to model temporal changes in marine scenes, thereby facilitating long-term navigation. By leveraging past visual information, this method enables robots to predict future states and adapt their paths accordingly. To address computational limitations, a new time-evolution function is designed that balances accuracy and efficiency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our method in terms of both accuracy and processing speed, thus enabling efficient long-term navigation in marine settings.

This study delves into the geometric properties of meromorphically isothermal surfaces, a concept that combines complex analytic functions with classical differential geometry. We establish the fundamental transformations of these surfaces, including meromorphic versions of the Darboux and Calapso transformations, and demonstrate that a meromorphic Gauss map implies a meromorphic mean curvature function. Furthermore, preserving a meromorphic Kuen surface property, such as its specific curvature properties, through a meromorphic Darboux transformation requires a specific condition on the involved functions.

Nonparametric regression estimation, particularly for complex conditional expectation functions, has been a significant area of study in statistics. The difficulty lies in the function's unknown characteristics, including smoothness and sparsity. The primary challenge is to determine the optimal estimation rate without knowing these properties. The "sparsity of interest" concept, which identifies the minimum level of zero sets, has been a significant focus. The "wiggles of interest" idea, which identifies the minimum number of zero derivatives, has also gained attention. The optimal estimation rate, which depends on these properties, has been a significant goal. The minimax risk lower bound, which represents the optimal estimation rate, has been a significant finding. The local polynomial fitting method, which is a leading technique, has been a significant approach. The optimal estimation rate, which depends on the penalty parameter, has been a significant finding. The penalty parameter selection methods, which are crucial for the estimation process, have been a significant area of study. The cross-validation and Pinsker penalty selection methods, which are two leading techniques, have been a significant finding. The Pinsker penalty method, which is a minimax risk estimator, has been a significant approach. The nonasymptotic risk bound, which represents the optimal estimation risk, has been a significant finding. The risk decomposition, which separates the bias and variance risks, has been a significant finding. The Pinsker penalty method, which is a minimax risk estimator, has been a significant approach.

A recent innovation by Kim et al. introduced the notion of $\lambda$-versions of r-Stirling numbers of the second kind, denoted as $\left\langle \begin{matrix} n \\ k \end{matrix} \right\rangle _{r,\lambda }$, which is a variant of Stirling numbers with added complexity. This paper delves into the properties of this new Stirling number variant and establishes identities related to it.

Predicting future relationships within a dynamic set of entities and their interactions is a key area of research in various fields such as medicine, social media analysis, and computer security. Temporal knowledge graphs, which capture entity relationships that evolve over time, are essential for this prediction task. However, existing methods for adding predicted connections to these graphs have limitations, particularly in their reliance on dynamic models that are difficult to train and their disregard for static entity relationships. This paper presents an innovative approach that overcomes these challenges by using pre-trained static models, trained on massive datasets of common entity relationships, to predict new connections. By combining this with a carefully selected subset of static models, our method achieves superior performance, outperforming existing techniques by a significant margin while also being more efficient and easier to use.

We examine the concept of robust equivalence among countable directed graphs, involving an equivalence relation that combines robust conjugacy and a predefined equivalence. This relates to a form of isomorphism for the associated graph group C*-algebras. We demonstrate that robust equivalence implies shift equivalence and equivalence robust equivalence are equivalent when the graphs have a maximum out-degree of two. Additionally, we establish that shift equivalence implies robust equivalence for graphs with an out-degree limit of three, providing counterexamples for the cases of out-degree two and unbounded max out-degree.

In a magnetically intense environment, the polarization of particles produced during the breakdown of unstable particles is altered. We've investigated the polarization of a top quark, the heaviest known particle, in a magnetic field. The top quark, despite its short lifespan, undergoes significant changes in a strong magnetic field, resulting in anisotropic particle fragmentation. Our research employs a general propagator approach to analyze the decay of top quarks and the subsequent particle production. The masses of the top quark and the W boson play a crucial role in the particle production process, and the width of the resonance affects the angular distribution of the particles. The magnetic field strength and the particle widths can cause anisotropy in the particle production process, and this anisotropy is more pronounced for certain helicity configurations. The anisotropy is more pronounced for configurations where the particles have the same helicity, and the effect is more significant for a magnetic field strength of 10^9 Tesla.

To effectively respond to complex queries in question-answering systems, language models require an in-depth understanding of connections between entities. Although pre-trained language models have shown impressive results in handling simple queries, they often struggle with more complex ones requiring the deduction of implicit relationships. This research introduces a novel approach that leverages a knowledge graph to augment a pre-trained language model in answering queries that require inferred knowledge. By incorporating a knowledge graph encoder and a transformer-based decoder, the model integrates inferred relationships between entities into its decision-making process. Experimental results on two datasets, including a modified Wikipedia question-answering dataset and a synthetic dataset, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in enhancing language models with deduced knowledge for accurate question answering.

In this research, we introduce a new class of highly interconnected graphs derived from nested sequences of groups, offering an efficient framework for random data generation and verification in a compact time frame. This paper builds upon a previous study that utilized abelian groups, extending the concept to non-abelian groups to broaden its applicability. We demonstrate that our graphs are (d, k+1)-expanders when k is less than or equal to a certain constant determined by d and the rank of the group, with a focus on non-abelian groups of a specific type.

This research investigates how effective different types of phrasing are in prompting GPT-3 for accurate responses on specific tasks without prior exposure to those details. We analyzed 12 GPT-3 prompts across 12 specific tasks, requiring participants to choose from three options, and found that certain phrasings can lead to a significant 10% increase in accuracy. We also discovered that the most effective general phrasing for our tested dataset is "Which of the following [sentence] best fits the description: [text description]?" with a 60.4% average accuracy rate.

We establish a connection between Artin motivations' L-invariants and those developed by Reguera by creating a specific Hodge realization of the Artin motive, which involves introducing an auxiliary element. The method builds upon similar approaches used in $\mathbb{L}$-invariants of adjoint families of modular forms by $\mathbb{L}$-invariants of adjoint families of modular forms by Darmon and Rotger and D. and L. R.

We've developed a novel technique for enhanced microwave signal detection in quantum systems using Rydberg atoms. This method leverages a camera to capture atomic fluorescence, which is then processed through a deep learning model to identify and isolate faint microwave-induced emissions. By training our image classifier on simulated data, we've achieved significant improvements over traditional signal averaging techniques, particularly when working with low signal-to-noise ratios. Our approach has also demonstrated resilience against variations in experimental conditions, such as changes in laser intensity and background noise levels, making it a versatile and adaptable detection method.

UGC 8839 is an exceptional spiral galaxy that exhibits a flat inner region with a significantly steeper light decline in its outer areas. By analyzing its properties, researchers have determined that this galaxy possesses a mass-to-light ratio of 0.74 +/- 0.07 in solar units, an extremely low value that suggests a unique composition. Furthermore, UUGC 8839's properties are consistent with those of a compact star cluster, an unusual feature for a galaxy of its size. By comparing its characteristics with theoretical models, scientists have been able to estimate the age and metallicity of UUGC 8839, finding an age of approximately 1.2 billion years and a low metallicity of -1.3 +/- 0.2 in solar units. The study also reveals that UUGC 8839's outer regions contain a significant amount of dust, which may have played a role in its unusual shape. The discovery of UUGC 8839's unique properties has significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution, as it suggests that star clusters can evolve into galaxies under certain conditions.

For quasiregular self-maps q of R^n, we calculate the Hausdorff dimension and measure of certain fractal sets within the hyperbolic space. These dimensions and measures depend on the dimension n, which must be at least 2.

The occurrence of gravity waves in the Martian atmosphere is well-established, and their impact on the thermosphere is evident. This study aims to quantify the characteristics of these gravity waves, specifically their spatial and temporal scales, and to evaluate how atmospheric conditions influence their behavior. By analyzing data from multiple spacecraft, we have determined that the typical spatial wavelength of these gravity waves ranges from 100 to 1000 km horizontally and 10 to 100 km vertically, with periods between 1 and 1000 minutes. Our results indicate that the horizontal propagation of these waves is restricted by atmospheric stability, and that their vertical propagation is limited to the mesosphere, with the exception of cases where they can reach the lower thermosphere under stable atmospheric conditions.

The LHC has established itself as the most powerful machine for generating photon-photon interactions at high energies. These interactions can be used to study fundamental physics, particularly in the context of quantum electrodynamics and the behavior of matter under extreme conditions. A recent study involving the ALICE detector at a collision energy of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions has provided new insights into forward charmonium production. These results align with predictions based on photoproduction mechanisms and a previously developed theoretical framework, providing a foundation for further research into the production of heavier systems and the study of nuclear structure.

The complexity of sound design has been significantly expanded by the development of audio synthesis techniques that utilize visual stimuli.  Traditional methods for generating visuals audibly rely on a manual process where artists adjust parameters to produce the desired sound.  This research introduces an innovative approach to controlling the synthesis of sound using visual inputs, reducing the need for manual parameter adjustments.  By utilizing a neural network, the system identifies the most influential factors affecting sound production and adjusts them automatically, resulting in coherent sound designs that align with the visual content.

In the realm of data analysis, sequences are increasingly prevalent, necessitating a method to capture the sequential temporal knowledge inherent in such data. Recent advancements in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have provided a means to do so, yet the extent to which they successfully acquire sequential temporal knowledge remains unclear. This research aims to address this knowledge gap by examining how RNNs learn to process sequential data, particularly in the context of machine learning applications. By developing a novel task that emphasizes sequential temporal knowledge and creating synthetic datasets with varying levels of such knowledge, we are able to investigate the mechanisms by which different types of RNNs learn to process sequential data. Our findings reveal that certain RNN architectures are capable of acquiring sequential temporal knowledge, whereas others struggle to do so, and that the manner in which they process information plays a crucial role in this phenomenon.

We've developed a model that quantifies the optimal timing and intensity of pandemic interventions, taking into account the specific conditions of a given situation. Our model, which is based on the SIR model, considers the specific parameters of a given scenario, such as the reproductive rate and the current levels of susceptible, infected, and recovered populations. We've found that the optimal timing and intensity of an intervention, such as lockdown, can be predicted with a high degree of accuracy, and that this prediction is generally applicable across a range of different scenarios.

In the context of machine learning pipelines, input data quality is a crucial factor that significantly influences model performance. Poor data can lead to model inaccuracies, making data troubleshooting a complex task. Existing methods for data evaluation often rely on individual model analysis, disregarding the interconnected nature of machine learning models. This paper introduces a novel approach called Significance of Data Inputs (SDI), which assesses the importance of specific data inputs in affecting model predictions. By considering machine learning pipelines as a cohesive system, SDI can accurately measure the impact of data on predictions, even in the presence of multiple interconnected models. Furthermore, SDI's efficiency is enhanced through the use of Shapley values, a technique that allows for rapid significance calculation. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SDI in pinpointing data inputs with the greatest influence on model predictions, outperforming current data evaluation methods.

This expository collection of notes covers four distinct but related research papers, each combining statistics, combinatorics, geometry, and algebra. The first paper, co-authored with Gessel, establishes a geometric proof of the Frobenius-Fischer identity by analyzing the action of the symmetric group on polynomials. The second paper provides a geometric proof of a combinatorial identity involving the enumeration of standard Young tableaux, based on the cohomology of Grassmannians. The third paper proves a geometric version of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra through analysis of Segre varieties. The fourth paper proves a combinatorial identity involving standard Young tableaux, based on Plucker relations in Grassmannians.

In materials with non-collinear magnetic arrangements, an unusual Hall effect has been observed, yet these structures are often fragile and susceptible to external influences such as pressure. A theoretical study of the material Mn$_3$Sn, an example of a triangular antiferromagnet, reveals that its anomalous Hall conductivity is largely dependent on the magnetic properties of the material, particularly its carrier concentration. Introducing pressure into Mn$_3$Sn causes its magnetic units to shift, resulting in an alteration of its electronic properties and an associated peak in its anomalous Hall conductivity. As pressure continues to increase, the material undergoes a phase transition, transitioning from a magnetic to a non-magnetic state, at which point its anomalous Hall conductivity diminishes.

In the field of Natural Language Processing, extracting relationships between entities within a text is a crucial task. Specifically, within biomedical domains, this process holds significant importance. The challenge lies in the fact thatunlike predefined categories, the potential relationship types between entities are unlimited. A widely accepted method for relation extraction involves defining a set of predefined relationship types, where a particular sentence or context is analyzed to determine the existence of a specified relationship. This paper delves into an in-depth examination of various neural network-based approaches for relation extraction, focusing on their architectures, the types of data they utilize, the methods for representing relationships, and the techniques for calculating confidence levels.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of a specific eigenvalue problem, known as the Steklov-Robin problem, which involves finding nontrivial pairs of a real-valued function and a real number that satisfy a particular differential equation and a corresponding boundary condition. We demonstrate that a unique sequence of increasing eigenvalues exists, along with corresponding eigenfunctions, and prove that this sequence behaves similarly to another known sequence of eigenvalues, while also establishing the orthogonality of the eigenfunctions.

We introduce a novel method for hypergraph reconstruction, enabling the efficient identification of a dense, distinct "core" within a sparse random graph that serves as its underlying hypergraph. Our approach leverages a "guided" algorithm, utilizing a simple yet effective sampling technique to achieve a semi-supervised reconstruction task with high accuracy. Specifically, our method accurately determines the hidden hypergraph using a limited number of strategically selected edges. Furthermore, we develop an unsupervised extension of the algorithm, which allows it to successfully reconstruct the hypergraph without access to any edges. Both variations of our algorithm can be implemented in polynomial time, and we illustrate the utility of our reconstruction technique by applying it to community detection and coding theory.

This research introduces a thorough understanding of chest X-rays by generating annotated images from computed tomography scans using standard radiographic settings. The proposed method leverages existing CT data, eliminating the need for additional scans or specialized equipment. A novel algorithm is employed to precisely position and orient CT projections to replicate the geometry of a conventional chest X-ray. The resulting annotated images provide radiologists with enhanced insights into the three-dimensional structure of the patient's chest, potentially improving diagnostic capabilities and reducing the need for follow-up CT scans.

The Thurston norm is a specific measure defined for a particular type of topological structure, and its precise values in relation to the Euler characteristic have been determined for a particular class of tight contact structures. This determination applies to manifolds of a particular topological form and has implications for understanding the properties of these tight contact structures.

Achieving directional light emission from lasers without using traditional reflective surfaces has been a long-standing objective in the field of microcavity lasers. In this research, a new method is developed based on entropy production rate to generate a non-equilibrium state and induce directional photon emission. The approach relies on a two-dimensional microcavity containing non-interacting excitons, where a specific type of entropy production is used to create an entropy gradient across the system. This gradient leads to an imbalance in the flow of entropy and results in directional photon emission. The study demonstrates that a higher entropy production rate in certain areas of the system correlates with increased emission intensity. Additionally, a relationship between entropy production and photon statistics is discovered, indicating that areas with higher entropy production tend to exhibit more ordered photon statistics.

This research evaluates the cost fluctuations of cryptocurrencies over time, comparing their behavior to traditional exchange markets. We've developed a new metric to measure cost instability and used it to analyze historical data from 2013 to 2019, covering both major and lesser-known digital currencies. Our findings indicate that most cryptocurrencies experienced significant price volatility during this period, with only a few, like Bitcoin and Ethereum, showing more stable behavior. We've also discovered that prices tend to stabilize after experiencing sudden drops, but this effect doesn't hold for all currencies. We've found that exchange periods with high trading activity result in more stable prices, with this effect being more pronounced in lesser-known cryptocurrencies. We've found that price instability is more prevalent during the initial stages of exchange periods, but this effect diminishes over time. We've found that exchange markets with high prices of a currency experience more volatility, with this effect being more pronounced in lesser-known cryptocurrencies. We've found that price movements often occur in a pattern, with this effect being more pronounced in lesser-known cryptocurrencies. We've found that exchange markets with high prices of a currency experience more significant price increases, with this effect being more pronounced in lesser-known cryptocurrencies. We've found that exchange markets with high prices of a currency experience more significant price movements, with this effect being more pronounced in lesser-known cryptocurrencies. We've found that exchange markets with high prices of a currency experience more significant price movements, with this effect being more pronounced in lesser-known cryptocurrencies.

We develop a discrete-time model that simulates the evolution of the KPZ equation, utilizing a matrix scattering equation whose reflection coefficient's magnitude is limited by a small parameter δ, akin to the linearized Burgers equation. By approximating the S-function with a constant δ and leveraging a series expansion in δ, we derive a formal solution to the discrete height model, ultimately transforming it into the expected Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble random matrix model through a large-time asymptotic analysis, thereby validating the noise theory at large times, although the nature of noise at intermediate times remains an open inquiry.

Our analysis of Magnetospheric Multi-Scale (MMS) spacecraft data reveals compressive turbulence within the solar wind, characterized by significant density fluctuations at sub-ion scales. This study utilized 10-minute intervals of in-situ measurements, including 42 events with strong turbulence and 40 control samples exhibiting typical ion-scale turbulence. We observed a consistent trend where the ratio of turbulent to total density variance increases as the rate of turbulent energy dissipation decreases, regardless of the turbulence generation mechanism. This pattern supports the concept of a multi-scale cascade process in which dissipation rates decline with increasing scale. Notably, the density variance exhibits a power-law relationship with the dissipation rate, characterized by a power-law exponent of approximately 0.5. This finding suggests that density variance is directly linked to electron-scale dissipation of turbulent energy.

X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) have the capability to generate intense, coherent attosecond pulses in the extreme ultraviolet and soft X-ray spectrum. The creation of such pulses relies heavily on the implementation of modified electron bunching techniques, which utilize a combination of radio-frequency (RF) and optical (OT) undulators. A crucial aspect of this process is the precise control of the energy-position (R56) of the electron bunch, which can be achieved through the application of a magnetic solenoid. The implementation of the altered chirp-taper method offers a viable approach to produce very short pulses, which can be further optimized by fine-tuning the electron bunch's characteristics. The present work outlines a strategy to generate intense, coherent attosecond pulses, which can be utilized to investigate ultrafast processes in solid-state materials and complex molecules.

The primary goal of this research is to examine how small-scale turbulence within the viscous lower layers of certain types of fluid flows influences their overall stability. This investigation builds upon the physical optics framework, a mathematical tool used in various fields to model complex systems. By applying this framework to an estimation of the turbulent effects above, specific equations have been derived that can be used to assess the typical size of these influences. The analysis indicates that turbulent nonlinearity is a crucial factor in this estimation. The results show that the typical size of turbulent nonlinearity is proportional to the square of the turbulent Reynolds number divided by its typical scale, a finding that is consistent with prior research. The typical size of turbulent nonlinearity is also compared to the typical size of turbulent advection, a measure of how turbulence interacts with the flow's velocity. The typical size of turbulent advection is estimated to be the turbulent Reynolds number divided by its typical scale. The typical size of turbulent advection is also compared to the typical size of turbulent production, a measure of how turbulence generates energy. The typical size of turbulent production is estimated to be the turbulent Reynolds number divided by its typical scale. The typical size of turbulent production is also compared to the typical size of turbulent dissipation, a measure of how turbulence dissipates energy. The typical size of turbulent dissipation is estimated to be the turbulent Reynolds number divided by its typical scale. We've developed a new method for quantifying electoral district manipulation by applying concepts from physics-based statistical mechanics to electoral data. This involves generating a distribution of districting plans, centered around an ideal map reflecting party affiliations, and produced through a process akin to heating and cooling. We define a metric to gauge the impact of district manipulation by measuring the temperature at which the distribution process ceases to produce varied plans. We apply this measure to both real and simulated voting data, and also to a set of actual districting plans for the lower house in New South Wales, Australia.

Identifying flaws in patterned textile images is a complex task due to the repetitive nature of the designs, which can mask irregularities. A novel approach is presented that uses a set of mathematical transformations to represent the image in a different format, revealing flaws that are not apparent in the original image. By applying a sparse representation to the transformed image, a simplified version is obtained, which can then be subtracted from the original to locate flaws. To handle the computational intensity of this process, a divide-and-conquer strategy is employed to partition the image into separate sections, allowing for faster processing. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in accurately identifying flaws in patterned textile images.

A reinforcement learning technique called SOFTRL, which incorporates information theory to create more predictable and consistent behavior in navigation agents, is being investigated. By maximizing the uncertainty of the choices made by the agent, an implicit bias is introduced that encourages the agent to stick to one course of action rather than randomly switching between options. This results in more coherent and predictable navigation patterns. Our research demonstrates that, despite the increased variability in individual trials, the overall performance of the agent is actually improved, with the agent tending to select the most effective path more frequently. This has the added benefit of reducing the amount of training required to achieve optimal results, as the agent's stabilized policy leads to more efficient learning.

This research establishes a minimum limit on the rate at which a star's mass is gathered from its surrounding environment, thereby setting a minimum bound on its Bondi mass reduction rate. The findings are relevant in setting a minimum age for pulsars and neutron stars, as well as in understanding the mass distribution of compact objects found in globular clusters.

Early on in galaxy development, the first stars likely formed within small, enclosed spaces like bulges or central star clusters at the heart of galaxies. Following the first stars' disappearance, these regions evolved into the nuclei of present-day galaxies, characterized by dense collections of stars orbiting supermassive black holes. Our study investigates how dense collections of stars interacting with the black hole produce gravitational waves, a phenomenon that can be detected by future space-based observatories. We find that the initial collections of stars produce significant gravitational waves, peaking at around 10^-3 Hz, a frequency range within the reach of such space-based detectors.

In modern power distribution networks, real-time monitoring is crucial for detecting and resolving issues before they escalate into significant outages. However, pinpointing the exact location of problems in these networks can be a complex task due to the sheer number of feeders and laterals involved. Our proposed solution leverages a data-driven approach to streamline the process of identifying and locating incidents in radial power distribution systems. Our method relies on real-time measurements of voltage and current at various nodes, utilizing a Bayesian framework to calculate the likelihood of incidents occurring on specific nodes. Our approach is validated through testing on a 33-node system and further demonstrated in its scalability on a larger 199-node system, showcasing its potential for practical application.

The decay of the $X(3872)$ into $J/\psi \pi \gamma$ is analyzed to determine its radiative width, and the results are used to discuss the nature of $X(3872)$. Additionally, the partial widths of the $X(3872)$ decaying into $J/\psi \pi\pi$ and $e^+e^-$ are calculated. The findings suggest that the mass difference between the $X(3872)$ and $J/\psi$ is primarily responsible for its radiative decay, and its dominant decay mode into $J/\psi \pi\pi$ involves a diphoton intermediate state. The calculated electric dipole and magnetic dipole partial widths for the $X(3872)$'s decay into $e^+e^-$ are found to be negligible.

For a smooth projective variety, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of an embedded quadric based on its coherent cohomology categories, generalizing previous work on Fano varieties with index at least two. Additionally, for varieties with such a quadric, we derive a precise formula for its degree.

Our new framework, TextWorldExpress, sets a groundbreaking record for text world generation competition by achieving a record 1.5 million environment steps simulated per second on a single GPU, surpassing previous limitations. Additionally, we've discovered that high simulation speeds have minimal impact on the policy learning rate, and our research reveals that imitation learning techniques are more effective than reinforcement learning methods in the text world generation domain.

To bypass the intricacies of Topological Insulators' description, we propose a method that sidesteps spatial dependencies, leveraging group theory and applying it to a 2D Topological Insulator model with imperfections.

We derive precise estimates for positive solutions of the p-Poisson equation in a sector of the plane with a finite angle. Our approach leverages the properties of the p-Poisson equation and employs a moving plane technique to establish sharp bounds. Additionally, we obtain novel estimates for positive solutions of the p-Poisson equation in a sector with an oscillating boundary.

This research introduces a novel spatial extreme value model that focuses on the most extreme conditional peaks of oceanic environments, using a Bayesian approach. We develop a Bayesian Cholesky decomposition method to estimate the model parameters and create confidence regions for the multivariate extremes. The proposed model is evaluated through simulations and a real-world case study examining the most extreme marine heatwaves in the Eastern Pacific Ocean between 2004 and 2019.

In 1994, Vojta introduced a conjecture proposing that for any non-constant function f from a set of rational points in affine n-space to the integers, there's a limited number of values it can take when its input is constrained by a certain degree-bound. This conjecture has been proven for specific cases when n equals 2 in the function field setting and when n equals 3 for all other function fields. This work confirms the same result for specific non-constant functions in affine n-space for all non-field base rings.

A recurring issue in robotics is the problem of domain shift, where data collected from one environment may not effectively train a model in a new, different environment. Robotics researchers have been developing solutions to address this challenge, but these solutions are often too specialized for robotics applications and not easily accessible to the broader computer vision community. We propose a novel approach to tackle this problem by leveraging human data for robotics tasks. Our method involves two key components: first, we use the C-VEX dataset to demonstrate that our approach can effectively transfer data from human operators to robots, even when there are significant differences in the data distributions. Second, we combine our transfer learning technique with a method called manifold-aware ICP to achieve even better results. Our solution is a valuable addition to the existing transfer learning literature, as it demonstrates the practical applicability of transfer learning in robotics tasks.

A study of the Higgs boson pair decay into a $b\bar{b}WW^*$ final state is conducted at 13 TeV in proton-proton collisions, utilizing the matrix element technique. The analysis incorporates the NLO QCD correction and a 2-body phase space approximation for the $W$ boson decay products, supplemented by parton shower and final state parton rejection to simulate the interaction at the LHC. The results are compared to existing predictions from other methods and the associated uncertainties are assessed.

Our research focuses on a fundamental aspect of 3D scene understanding, specifically how to determine the orientation of objects within those scenes. To address this challenge, we developed a self-supervised approach that utilizes unsupervised data to train a model for 3D object localization. By leveraging widely-used datasets, we discovered that the task of finding an object's position is interconnected with recognizing its orientation, thus enabling the use of unlabelled data for training. To validate our method, we conducted experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and observed superior performance compared to the existing best unsupervised approaches.

A growing number of social media users are encountering and disseminating false information on platforms like Twitter, which can have severe implications for society. To address this challenge, researchers have focused on identifying and mitigating misinformation spread in online discussions. This paper aims to expand upon existing work by tackling the under-explored task of classifying user responses within a conversation thread regarding misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines on Twitter. By developing a new dataset comprising real-world misinformation targetting vaccines, we aim to fill a critical gap in the current literature. Our approach involves creating a comprehensive dataset of Twitter conversations surrounding COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, and we evaluate its efficacy by comparing various machine learning models in classifying user responses within these threads. Our findings reveal that models leveraging pre-trained language representations and incorporating conversation context outperform those that do not, and our code and data will be made available upon request.

A new method has been developed to create extremely short bursts of light, lasting only a few hundred attoseconds, using a rare gas in a strong field. By taking advantage of the unique properties of this strong field, researchers were able to generate these bursts with greater stability and control, even in the absence of complex computer models. The resulting light bursts contain significant harmonics, which can be amplified and combined to create even shorter bursts of light. The length of these bursts can be controlled by adjusting the strength of the field, offering a precise way to manipulate light on an incredibly small scale.

We've conducted a comprehensive study of the binary star system Algol using high-quality spectra from the VLT and the Keck telescopes. By examining the companion stars of F and G, we found that their spectra resemble those of K-type stars with surface temperatures around 4000-4500 K. Our analysis revealed no signs of cooler objects or irregularities in their light curves, contradicting previous findings. By comparing the line broadening of these companions to that of other known systems, we determined their radii to be approximately 1.3-1.5 times the radius of the sun. Our results confirm that the companions are likely main-sequence stars, and we attribute the discrepancies with previous studies to the limited quality of the original spectra. Our findings have been incorporated into the standard model of Algol's evolution, and our study serves as a template for similar investigations of other eclipsing binary star systems.

This paper investigates a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with an energy-dissipating condition, set in the external region of a bounded, convex area. We establish that for initial data exceeding a critical threshold, the initial value problem has no global solutions, implying the solutions 'explode' in finite time. The derived critical value is data-dependent and can be quite low in contrast to previously established fixed critical values in similar studies.

Physically-informed neural networks (PINNs) are a novel class of machine learning models that can solve partial differential equations by incorporating physical laws into a data-driven framework. A significant challenge in PINNs is accurately predicting solutions, particularly in regions with high solution gradients. To address this limitation, various strategies have been proposed, including the introduction of auxiliary functions. In this study, a new vertex creation method based on residual analysis is presented to dynamically create new neurons in regions where the solution is not being predicted accurately. By using the residual of the physical operator, the proposed method identifies areas requiring the introduction of new neurons and uses a cosine function to define their spatial influence. Through a comprehensive set of numerical experiments, the effectiveness of this adaptive vertex creation method is demonstrated in solving various differential equations and multi-physics problems.

A novel type of nonvolatile transistor, the ferroelectric transistor (FeFET), has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional transistors. The development of multi-domain FeFETs has been proposed to enhance their performance by mitigating the short channel effect and reducing adverse capacitance. In this research, a multi-domain FeFET simulation model was developed to analyze the device's performance. The results indicate that the presence of domain walls within the ferroelectric layer can create a localized negative charge, affecting the device's capacitance characteristics.

A freight ecosystem dependency-weakness knowledge graph is created to model the interconnected nature of freight ecosystem elements through two types of relationships.  The "dependency" relationship represents connections between different components, such as a port's reliance on a railway for freight transport, while the "weakness" relationship represents connections between different elements, such as a freight forwarder's competition level or a pipeline's transportation capacity.  The freight ecosystem knowledge graph is developed using a combination of public data and a general approach that can be applied to other freight ecosystem knowledge graphs.  A method for propagating weaknesses along elements of the freight ecosystem is also proposed, which can be used to identify and address potential disruptions within the ecosystem.

We examine the properties of ergodicity in a stochastic version of the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation that experiences sudden jumps in its behavior. This happens when the noise in the system only occurs at specific points in space, leading to discontinuous changes in the solution. To study this, we first establish that small disturbances in the system can't be reduced to simpler components, a concept known as irreducibility. This is done using a mathematical approach that involves looking at how the system's external forces interact with its exterior boundaries. Based on this result, we then prove that the system reaches a stable equilibrium over time, a concept known as ergodicity. This is shown to hold true under certain conditions, including when the system's noise has a specific type of distribution. This proof of ergodicity has important applications in understanding how similar systems, such as those with localized coherence in optical cavities, behave in the long run.

A power graph of a group G is defined based on a relationship where two elements are connected if one is a power of the other. The minimum degree of this graph represents the smallest number of connections any single vertex has. In the case of a finite nilpotent group, a question arises as to the power graph's minimum degree. We've discovered that for a finite nilpotent group G, the minimum degree is less than or equal to the sum of specific values related to G's prime power order components. Furthermore, for a finite abelian p-group, the minimum degree is precisely determined. We've also identified conditions under which the minimum degree equals a certain value in a direct product of two p-groups.

A novel hadron spectrometer is being developed to gather precise data on the characteristics of cosmic-ray particles in an effort to create an advanced profile of their intensity and composition. This information will serve as a foundation for enhancing our understanding of the physical processes that govern the acceleration and development of particles at the top of the Earth's atmosphere. By utilizing cutting-edge detection methods and advanced data analysis techniques, this spectrometer aims to provide groundbreaking insights into the behavior of high-energy particles.

We introduce a novel type of neural network, orientation convolutive networks (OCNs), which are invariant to the orientation of input images without requiring additional training. OCNs utilize a unique set of filters, derived from the convolution theorem, to process input data and are mathematically grounded in Fourier domain analysis. The proposed OCN model is further enhanced by incorporating a FCN layer, which is also mathematically justified. Experimental evaluations on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

Deep learning techniques, particularly graph convolutional networks (GCNs), have shown great potential in processing 3D data, including point clouds and graph-structured information. However, designing effective GCNs for point cloud processing remains a complex task, as existing methods often struggle to balance performance and efficiency. To address this challenge, this paper presents a comprehensive analysis of GCNs for 3D point cloud processing, focusing on the convolution operation and its impact on performance. By investigating the graph convolution, graph convolutions with linear filters, and max-pooling based graph convolutions, this research sheds light on their respective advantages and limitations. Based on these findings, a new graph convolutional network framework, called G^2N, is proposed, which integrates a graph convolutions with linear filters layer and a max-pooling based graph convolutions layer to effectively capture both local and global features. G^2N is then evaluated on four widely-used benchmarks, where it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in various 3D object recognition tasks.

To safeguard Mobile Operating Systems from malicious applications, signature-based detection methods have been employed, yet they fall short in identifying novel trojan variants. A potential solution involves leveraging app functionality to detect malicious apps, but this is hindered by the diversity of mobile operating systems and the multitude of available applications, making direct analysis impractical. In response, a signature-based approach focusing on mobile app behavioral patterns rather than specific functionalities has been proposed. By representing behavioral patterns using a graph structure, a signature database can be built to facilitate Trojan variant identification. However, existing graph-based methods are limited in their ability to account for graph size variations and node structure differences, leading to suboptimal results. To address these limitations, a novel graph-based detection method, known as SHTE, has been developed. SHTE utilizes the Weisfeiler-Lehman kernel to compare graphs of varying sizes and structures, and a corresponding database, known as SHTE DB, has been constructed to demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in mobile Trojan variant detection.

We introduce an upgrade to the integral field module used in the Magellan IMACS Spectrograph, known as ROSIE. This integral field unit, initially designed to capture light from a 1.5-degree field of view, has been successfully operating on the Magellan IMACS Spectrograph since 2011. However, due to wear and tear, the original ROSIE was taken apart and one of its halves was replaced. To maintain optimal performance, the two sections were recombined and realigned. To verify the quality of the images, we conducted a series of tests using both artificial stars and actual astronomical targets. Our analysis shows that the upgraded ROSIE now produces high-quality 2D spectra with excellent resolution and accurate color accuracy.

Our research has found that carbon-carbon fusion at low energies exhibits complex dynamics, characterized by oscillations in cross-sections. To better understand this, we employed the Trojan horse method, a technique typically used for direct reactions, to measure the fusion cross-sections. Our findings reveal that applying this technique requires careful consideration of the entrance channel's structure and statistical properties. We have developed a new approach to implement this technique, taking into account the necessary corrections, and our results are in line with direct measurements and theoretical predictions.

The study of exoplanet interiors is a crucial area of research, yet it is limited by a lack of observational data. To address this limitation, researchers have developed a method to utilize the well-established chemical compositions of host stars as a means of predicting the bulk compositions of exoplanets. By applying this approach, the team has created a database of 1,000 models of exoplanets with masses ranging from 0.1 to 10 Earth masses. These models are based on the assumption that the volatile elements of exoplanets adhere to the solar composition, while refractory elements vary according to the host star's composition. The results indicate that the bulk density of an exoplanet is significantly influenced by its volatile content, which is in turn determined by the star's metallicity for refractory-rich terrestrial planets. However, this relationship is less pronounced for water-rich exoplanets. Furthermore, the study found that the bulk density of terrestrial planets with masses less than 1.5 Earth masses is largely independent of their composition, with variations of less than 10%.

Current indoor wireless communication systems can also collect comprehensive data on the environment through channel state information (CSI), which can be utilized to accurately determine the user's location. Nevertheless, CSI is highly susceptible to interference from external factors, such as body movements and object shifts, thereby compromising localization precision. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel method that leverages attention mechanisms to isolate and eliminate relevant features from CSI, thereby enhancing localization precision. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a notable improvement in localization accuracy compared to existing approaches, with a substantial reduction in mean absolute error (from 0.53m to 0.25m) in a real-world WiFi localization testbed.

This work, along with a companion paper, aims to provide a comprehensive library for modal reasoning by defining the fundamental properties of various topological structures and creating a set of basic modal languages on top of these structures. The library, which is organized around six distinct topological components, will allow for the reasoning and proof of modal axioms through a unified approach, thereby serving as a foundational tool for further research in modal reasoning.

A graph's edges are treated as colored edges when given a specific color. The term "edge-tinting" refers to assigning colors to a graph's edges so that every vertex has an equal number of colored edges in each color category. Researchers have discovered that bipartite cubic graphs do not always have an edge-tinting in five different colors. However, it is known that such graphs do have an edge-tinting in five different colors if they contain at least one triangle. We present an example of a five different colored, robustly 5-edge-tintable bipartite cubic graph.

The function f is said to be non-negative if f_x has no negative values. The function f is said to be spectrally restricted if the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of f_x are all less than or equal to some value λ.
